overview:
The congregation weeps all night, wishes it had died in Egypt or in the wilderness, and talks of choosing a captain to lead it back. Joshua and Caleb plead that the land is good and the LORD is with them, and the people are about to stone them when the glory of the LORD appears. The LORD threatens to destroy Israel and make a nation of Moses. Moses pleads, and the LORD pardons, but he swears that no one of this generation except Caleb and Joshua will see the land. They will wander forty years, a year for each day of the search, and the ten spies die by plague. The next morning the people go up to fight anyway and are beaten back to Hormah.

Moses' prayer works by quoting. In vv. 17–18 he repeats the words the LORD proclaimed about himself at Sinai (Exodus 34:6–7) and asks him to act on them.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars see Numbers as compiled later from older and priestly sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The night and days after the spies return, in the second year after the Exodus; the forty years begin here. Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts the Exodus about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer about 1250 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The camp at Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran (13:26). The failed attack goes up into the hill country of the Negev and ends at Hormah (v. 45).

hermeneutics:
Moses' argument in vv. 13–16 assumes that the nations read a people's fortunes as the record of its god. About 840 BC the Moabite king Mesha explained on his victory stele why Omri of Israel had oppressed Moab for many days: Chemosh, Moab's god, was angry with his land. When Mesha won the land back, that too was Chemosh's doing. In that world a people's death in the desert would be read as its god's anger or as its god's weakness. Moses fears that Egypt and Canaan will choose weakness, and he asks the LORD to guard his name.

The same stele says Israel held the district of Medeba through Omri's days and half the days of his son, “forty years.” The figure does not match the biblical reigns closely, and it works as a round number for a generation. The sentence of vv. 33–34 uses that span with a precise rule, a year for each day of the search, so that the generation that refused the land lives out its life outside it.

Mesha also goes to war only when his god sends him. Chemosh says to him, “Go, take Nebo from Israel,” and he goes by night and takes it. In such a world an army that marched without its god's word was asking for defeat. Verses 40–45 show Israel doing exactly that: the people go up after the LORD has said not to, while the ark of the covenant and Moses stay in the camp.

notes: **The hinge is v. 28:** “as ye have spoken in mine ears, so will I do” to you. The sentence grants the people's own wish.

**Fall:** the verb comes 5 times. The people fear they will fall by the sword (v. 3), Moses and Aaron fall on their faces (v. 5), carcases will fall in the wilderness (vv. 29, 32), and Moses warns the attackers that they will fall by the sword (v. 43).
**Murmur** comes 6 times (vv. 2, 27 ×3, 29, 36), and “forty” 3 times in vv. 33–34, matching the forty days of 13:25.

The chapter closes the spies unit begun at 13:1 and turns the book. The generation counted in chs. 1–4 is now sentenced to die in the wilderness. The second census in ch. 26 counts their children, and 26:64–65 confirms that only Caleb and Joshua were left.

**Backward and forward:** Moses' plea follows the pattern of his plea after the golden calf, where he also asks what the Egyptians would say (Exodus 32:11–14). Psalm 95:10–11 turns the oath of this chapter into a warning for every later generation.

traditions.text: This revelation on priesthood reads the wilderness oath as the loss of more than a land. Moses sought to sanctify the people so that they might behold the face of God, but they hardened their hearts, and the Lord swore that they would not enter his rest while in the wilderness, “which rest is the fulness of his glory.” So he took Moses and the Holy Priesthood from their midst, and the lesser priesthood continued.

traditions.date: c. 544 BC and c. 82 BC (Book of Mormon)
traditions.text: Two Book of Mormon preachers use the wilderness oath, in the language of Psalm 95, as a warning to their own people. Jacob labored to bring his people into God's rest, “lest by any means he should swear in his wrath” that they should not enter, as in the provocation in the wilderness. Alma calls Israel's rebellion the first provocation and urges his hearers not to harden their hearts but to enter the rest of God.

In his praise of Israel's famous men, Ben Sira honors Joshua and Caleb for standing against the congregation in Moses' days. They turned away wrath and stopped the evil report, and so of six hundred thousand men on foot only these two were kept alive to bring the people into the land flowing with milk and honey. He adds that Caleb kept his strength into old age, as Joshua 14:11 says.

Pirkei Avot sets the “ten times” of v. 22 in a list of tens: ten miracles in Egypt and ten at the sea, ten plagues in Egypt and ten at the sea, and ten trials by which the fathers tried God in the wilderness. The Talmud adds that the sentence was sealed by the spies' words in particular. If those who slandered wood and stones were punished so, it reasons, how much more one who slanders a person.

The Mishnah counts the decree that the fathers would die in the wilderness as the first of five disasters on the Ninth of Av, the day the Temple later fell twice. The Talmud explains the date from v. 1: the people wept that night for nothing, so God said he would give them a reason to weep on it for generations.

Did the wilderness generation lose the world to come as well as the land? Rabbi Akiva said yes, reading v. 35 in two parts: “consumed” in this world, “there they shall die” in the next. Rabbi Eliezer disagreed and applied Psalm 50:5 to them: they were the ones who made a covenant with God by sacrifice.

Jewish law requires ten men for public prayer, and the Talmud finds the number here. The LORD calls the ten spies an “evil congregation” (v. 27), since Joshua and Caleb are not counted, so a congregation is ten. The quorum for sanctifying God's name was learned from the men who brought the evil report. The same chain of reasoning links the spies to Korah's company in ch. 16, also called a congregation.

Josephus explains the attack of vv. 40–45 as pride. The people decided they could win without Moses, claiming that God's help came from their ancestors' merit and their own virtue, and went out “not waiting for any assistance from their legislator.” Beaten and chased back to the camp, they took the defeat as God's anger and accepted Moses' leadership again. Moses then led them further into the wilderness, away from the Canaanites, to wait for a better time.

Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and asks who the rebels were: all who came out of Egypt with Moses, “whose carcases fell in the wilderness,” which echoes v. 29. They could not enter because of unbelief. Even Joshua (KJV “Jesus”), who did lead the next generation in, did not give them the final rest, so that rest is still offered “to day,” and the writer warns his readers not to fall short of it the same way.

Paul counts the wilderness deaths among the warnings for the church: God was not pleased with many of them, and they were overthrown in the wilderness, and Christians should not murmur as some of them did. Jude uses the same history against false teachers: the Lord saved a people out of Egypt and afterward destroyed those who did not believe.
